questions.prompt: What does \(H\le G\) mean?
questions.answer: It means \(H\) is a subgroup of \(G\). The subset \(H\) is itself a group using the same operation as \(G\).

questions.prompt: Does a subgroup use a new operation or the parent group's operation \(*\)?
questions.answer: A subgroup uses the parent group's operation. It is not allowed to invent a different operation on the subset.

questions.prompt: Name one subgroup of \((\mathbb Z,+)\).
questions.answer: The even integers \(2\mathbb Z\) form a subgroup of \((\mathbb Z,+)\). They contain \(0\), are closed under addition, and contain additive inverses.

questions.prompt: What identity element must a subgroup of \((\mathbb Z,+)\) contain?
questions.answer: It must contain the parent identity, which is \(0\). A subgroup cannot choose a different identity from the one used in the parent group.

questions.prompt: Show that \(2\mathbb Z\) is closed under addition.
questions.answer: Let \(2m,2n\in2\mathbb Z\), where \(m,n\in\mathbb Z\). Then \(2m+2n=2(m+n)\). Since \(m+n\in\mathbb Z\), the sum is in \(2\mathbb Z\).

questions.prompt: Show that \(2\mathbb Z\) is closed under additive inverses.
questions.answer: Let \(2m\in2\mathbb Z\). Its additive inverse is \(-(2m)=2(-m)\). Since \(-m\in\mathbb Z\), the inverse is also in \(2\mathbb Z\).

questions.prompt: Is \(\{1,-1\}\) a subgroup of the non-zero real numbers under multiplication?
questions.answer: Yes. It is non-empty, products stay in the set, and each element is its own multiplicative inverse. It uses the same multiplication operation as the parent group.

questions.prompt: Why is \(\{1,2\}\) not a subgroup of the non-zero real numbers under multiplication?

questions.prompt: Test whether \(3\mathbb Z\) is a subgroup of \((\mathbb Z,+)\).
questions.answer: It is non-empty because \(0=3\cdot0\in3\mathbb Z\). If \(3m,3n\in3\mathbb Z\), then \(3m+3n=3(m+n)\in3\mathbb Z\). The inverse of \(3m\) is \(-3m=3(-m)\in3\mathbb Z\). Therefore \(3\mathbb Z\le\mathbb Z\).

questions.prompt: Test whether the positive integers are a subgroup of \((\mathbb Z,+)\).
questions.answer: The positive integers do not contain the parent identity \(0\). Also, the inverse of \(1\) under addition is \(-1\), which is not positive. Therefore they are not a subgroup of \((\mathbb Z,+)\).

questions.prompt: Why does associativity not need a new proof when testing a subgroup \(H\le G\)?
questions.answer: The subgroup uses the same operation as \(G\). Since associativity holds for all elements of \(G\), it automatically holds for the elements of \(H\), which are also elements of \(G\).

questions.prompt: In \(D_4\), explain why \(\{e,r,r^2,r^3\}\) is a subgroup.
questions.answer: This subset contains the identity \(e\). Products of rotations are rotations, so it is closed. The inverse of \(r^k\) is \(r^{4-k}\) modulo \(4\), which is also in the subset. Associativity is inherited from \(D_4\).

questions.prompt: Test whether \(\{e,r^2\}\) is a subgroup of the rotations of a square.
questions.answer: The set contains \(e\). Closure holds because \(r^2r^2=r^4=e\), and multiplying by \(e\) changes nothing. Each element is its own inverse: \(e^{-1}=e\) and \((r^2)^{-1}=r^2\). Hence it is a subgroup.

questions.prompt: Test whether \(\{e,s\}\) is a subgroup of a dihedral group when \(s\) is a reflection.
questions.answer: It contains \(e\). Since \(s^2=e\), products of elements in \(\{e,s\}\) remain in \(\{e,s\}\). Also \(s^{-1}=s\) and \(e^{-1}=e\). Associativity is inherited, so \(\{e,s\}\) is a subgroup.

questions.prompt: Show that the intersection of two subgroups \(H\) and \(K\) of \(G\) is a subgroup of \(G\).
questions.answer: Both \(H\) and \(K\) contain \(e\), so \(H\cap K\) is non-empty. If \(a,b\in H\cap K\), then they are in both subgroups, so \(ab\in H\) and \(ab\in K\); hence \(ab\in H\cap K\). If \(a\in H\cap K\), then \(a^{-1}\) is in both \(H\) and \(K\). Thus \(H\cap K\le G\).

questions.prompt: Why is the union of two subgroups not always a subgroup? Give an example in \((\mathbb Z,+)\).
questions.answer: Take \(2\mathbb Z\) and \(3\mathbb Z\). Both are subgroups. But \(2\in2\mathbb Z\) and \(3\in3\mathbb Z\), so both are in the union, while \(2+3=5\) is in neither \(2\mathbb Z\) nor \(3\mathbb Z\). The union is not closed, so it is not a subgroup.

questions.prompt: Let \(H\) be a non-empty finite subset of a group \(G\) that is closed under products. Explain why \(H\) is a subgroup.
questions.answer: Choose \(h\in H\). Since \(H\) is finite and closed under products, the powers \(h,h^2,h^3,\ldots\) must eventually repeat. Cancellation in \(G\) gives a positive power \(h^k=e\), so \(e\in H\). Then \(h^{k-1}\in H\) and \(h h^{k-1}=e\), so \(h^{-1}\in H\). Thus inverses exist in \(H\), and \(H\le G\).

questions.prompt: A student tests a subgroup candidate by changing multiplication to addition inside the subset. Diagnose the error.
questions.answer: A subgroup must use the same operation \(*\) as the parent group. Changing the operation creates a different algebraic structure and does not prove anything about being a subgroup of the original group. The subset must be tested using the parent operation only.

questions.prompt: Prove that every subgroup contains the parent identity.
questions.answer: Let \(H\le G\). Since \(H\) is a group under the same operation, it has an identity, say \(e_H\). For any \(h\in H\), the equation \(e_Hh=h\) holds. In the parent group, the identity satisfying this role is unique, so \(e_H=e_G\). Therefore the subgroup contains the parent identity.

questions.prompt: If \(H\le G\) and \(g\in G\), why is the set \(gHg^{-1}=\{ghg^{-1}:h\in H\}\) a subgroup?
questions.answer: It is non-empty because \(geg^{-1}=e\) is included. If \(gh_1g^{-1}\) and \(gh_2g^{-1}\) are elements, their product is \(gh_1g^{-1}gh_2g^{-1}=g(h_1h_2)g^{-1}\), and \(h_1h_2\in H\). The inverse of \(ghg^{-1}\) is \(g h^{-1} g^{-1}\), and \(h^{-1}\in H\). Therefore the set is a subgroup.
